scope: Independent review of 13 proposed corrections, 21 contextual items, and 11 unresolved terms from audit-lingo.json.
notes: Original authored coaching articles count as primary sources for coaching terminology; tournament/Tour accounts provide primary usage evidence.
Strategy remains contextual even when proposed wording is factually defensible. This review does not turn tactical preferences into universal facts.

replacement.explain: Evert built her game around baseline consistency, while Navratilova attacked with serve-and-volley tennis. Their contrasting styles made their rivalry distinctive.

entries.rationale: Independently reviewed replacement; Opponent backhand depends on opponent handedness.

replacement.explain: A right-handed player runs around the backhand side and hits a forehand diagonally toward the opposing ad court. That is a right-handed opponent’s backhand side, but a left-hander’s forehand side.

entries.rationale: Independently reviewed replacement; Diagonal is sqrt(78²+27²)=82.54 ft; posts are outside sidelines, so net-post height is not down-the-line crossing height.

replacement.explain: The full singles-court diagonal is about 82.5 feet, versus 78 feet along a sideline. A crosscourt ball also travels over the lower central part of the net. These margins often make it a safer rally direction.

entries.rationale: Independently reviewed replacement; Open-court pattern depends on return quality; hitting behind is not exclusive to a T serve.

replacement.question: After a wide deuce-court serve pulls the returner off court and produces an attackable return, which common serve-plus-one pattern uses the open space?
replacement.explain: One common pattern is wide serve, then attack the open court. Return quality and the opponent’s recovery can make another target preferable.

entries.rationale: Independently reviewed replacement; Percentage must be attributed rather than asserted for every professional match.

replacement.question: In Craig O’Shannessy’s published Brain Game rally-length breakdown, approximately what share of points fall in the 0–4-shot category?
replacement.explain: That published breakdown gives roughly 70% to 0–4 shots. It is a coaching benchmark, not a fixed percentage for every match or level.

entries.rationale: Independently reviewed replacement; Original side reference is ambiguous.

choices: To the exact centre hash every time
Toward a position that covers the opponent’s reply angles, usually short of the centre mark after a wide crosscourt
All the way to the opposite alley
Stand still and admire it
replacement.explain: After a wide crosscourt from the baseline, recover toward the middle while shading toward the likely crosscourt reply. The best position changes with the opponent’s contact point and available angles.

entries.rationale: Independently reviewed replacement; Magnus acts in flight, not as upward bounce force.

replacement.explain: A typical heavy topspin ball can rebound high because of its incoming trajectory and interaction with the court. Bounce also depends on speed, angle and surface; the Magnus force acts during flight.

entries.rationale: Independently reviewed replacement; Original confuses semi-western bevel 4 with full western; omit extraneous numbering.

replacement.explain: A Western forehand grip is associated with topspin-oriented forehands. Semi-Western is a different grip; grip alone does not create spin.

entries.rationale: Numbering needs the viewing direction as well as clockwise/top-face convention; otherwise mirror interpretation remains possible.

replacement.question: Viewed from the butt cap toward the racket head, using eight-bevel numbering with the top face as 1 and counting clockwise, a right-handed eastern forehand grip places the index-finger base knuckle…
replacement.explain: On bevel 3 for a right-hander under that numbering convention. A left-handed grip mirrors the position.

entries.rationale: Independently reviewed replacement; I is a formation, not a court name; break points can occur on deuce side.

replacement.question: In doubles, what do “deuce court” and “ad court” mean?
choices: Indoor and advantage sets
The right-hand and left-hand halves respectively, viewed from each player’s own end facing the net
Italy and Adelaide
First serve and second serve
replacement.explain: Deuce is the right half and ad is the left half from your own end facing the net. “I-formation” names a doubles formation, not a court. Break points can be played on either half.

entries.rationale: Independently reviewed replacement; Holding every service game is sufficient but not necessary; exchanged breaks can restore on-serve state.

choices: Neither player has a net service-break advantage in the set
One player necessarily leads by a service break
A tiebreak must be in progress
The umpire is serving
replacement.explain: A set can be on serve after both players hold or after they exchange breaks. It does not require every service game to have been held.

entries.rationale: Independently reviewed replacement; Original confuses receiver handedness with server handedness.

choices: A sharply angled slice serve, typically wide from the deuce court for a right-handed server or ad court for a left-handed server
A kick serve into the body
An underhand serve
A second-serve moonball
replacement.explain: The nickname describes a wide slice that pulls the returner away from the court; the usual serving side depends on the server’s handedness.

entries.rationale: Independently reviewed replacement; Direction is not part of kick-serve definition.

choices: A serve with a topspin component that produces a high bounce
A flat bomb only
A drop serve
Illegal spin
replacement.explain: A kick serve uses a topspin component to help the ball dip into the box and rebound high; it is not defined by a particular target.

entries.rationale: Independently reviewed replacement; Australian formation original describes the opposite half ambiguously.

choices: The server and net partner start on the same lateral half of their own court
Both players at net before the serve
Two-handed return only
A tiebreak format
replacement.explain: The server’s partner starts on the same side as the server, typically across from the opposing net player. The server usually stands nearer the centre mark.

entries.rationale: Direct original coaching article by Ron Waite defines the high, topspin, deep ball; original explanation saying it steals time is misleading.

replacement.explain: A moonball is a high, looping groundstroke, usually with topspin and depth. It can push the opponent back and change the rally’s rhythm.

entries.rationale: Direct coaching source defines the high topspin groundstroke.

Direct WTA match account confirms playing behind a moving opponent; deliberate disguise is not required.

replacement.explain: Wrong-footing means sending the ball behind an opponent who has already committed to moving the other way.

entries.rationale: WTA describes wrong-footing as hitting behind Muchova while she moves to cover the opposite side.
US Open explicitly refers to Jimmy Connors as Jimbo.
Original coaching resource by Wayne Elderton explicitly defines body placement as a serve that jams the returner.
USTA uses dead ball for a serve that is out of play; ITF Rule 11 defines when a ball remains in play.
Original instruction by coach Doug King defines a short sitter as an attackable ball with time to set up, preferably above net height.
Original coaching handout hosted by Tennis Australia explicitly describes shanking balls off the racket frame.
